text: Hi there. Today we're going to talk about spotting misleading charts, and I think you'll find it helps you more often than you'd expect. You've probably scrolled past a chart today that was quietly lying to you. Let me sketch one, kind of like you'd see on the news. The title is 'Crime Is Skyrocketing!' and there are two bars. Let me pick a red-- yes, red for the tall one. It looks about five times taller than the other bar. Scary, right? But what if I told you the two numbers are 52 and 50? Same chart, very different story. Let's figure out how that happens.

Think about the last bar chart you looked at. You probably read the bar heights first and the axis labels second, if at all. Let's use that habit against ourselves. Say bar A is 52 burglaries per 1,000 and bar B is 50 per 1,000. I'll draw the axis in a red-- actually, let me grab a green marker, and I'll start it at 49. Now A is 3 units tall, because 52 minus 49 is 3, and B is 1 unit tall. A looks 3 times as tall. Remember our crime headline from a moment ago? That's the same trick. But what happens if the axis starts at 0? Redrawn, A and B look almost the same height. To put a number on the real difference, I'd write delta equals 52 minus 50, so delta is 2. Then 2 divided by 50 is 0.04, or 4 percent. A small difference dressed up as a big one. Coming up, we'll draw both side by side.

Let's draw this together. I'll fold the page in half, sort of, so we get two panels. In the left panel, I'll draw the axis from 49 to 53, and then bars A and B. A reaches 52, B reaches 50, and the gap looks dramatic. I'll write 'Zoomed' underneath. Over on the right, the axis goes from 0 to 60, and when I draw A and B again, they're nearly level. That panel is 'Honest.' Now, the thing I want you to notice is the baseline. I'd take this orange-- hmm, let me use blue so it stands out. I'll circle the baseline on the left, at 49, and then the one on the right, at 0. Remember our delta of 2? It's the same 2 in both panels. Only the circled spot is different.

Here's the idea behind that blue circle, stated plainly. We would define a misleading chart as one where the visual change is bigger or smaller than the real change in the numbers. A chart's visual size should be proportional to the quantity it represents. Edward Tufte named a way to measure this, the lie factor, which is the size of the effect shown in the graphic divided by the size of the effect in the data. Let me write that under the left panel. The graphic shows a 200% jump, but the data show 4%, because our delta of 2 over 50 is 0.04. So 200 divided by 4 is 50. That's a chart stretching the truth fifty times over.

So we've handled bars, and you probably feel pretty good about spotting a stretched axis. But what if the axis is perfectly honest and the chart still misleads you? Let me sketch a line, a town's monthly unemployment rate, 5.1% down to 4.9% across 3 months. Nothing is stretched here. Now I'll draw the same data over 10 years, sort of zoomed way out. Same numbers, different impression. That's the puzzle we're going to untangle next, and I think you'll enjoy it.

Let's try a worked example, and I'd encourage you to do the arithmetic along with me. Say a company ad shouts, our stock is up 30%! Here's the claim: on March 1 the price was $100, and on June 1 it was $130. Thirty over 100 is 30%, so the math checks out. But what if we asked, up compared to when? Let me draw the full year, in blue, no, let me pick green for the window. In January the stock sat at $200, then it fell to $100 by March. That's the drop the ad skips. Now I'll draw a small green box around March through June, just a sliver of the curve. To get the full-year change, we do 130 minus 200, which is negative 70, divided by 200, giving us negative 35%. Down 35%, not up 30%! Remember the zoomed panel? Same trick, different axis: time. The numbers were honest, but the window was chosen very carefully, and you'd probably never notice unless you asked to see the whole line.

So what do you take away from the stock ad? Let's say you just remember three questions, and I'll write them on the board now. Where does the axis start? What window of time? Compared to what? Ask those whenever a chart looks too good, or too scary. In the next video, we'll look at how the word "average" can mean mean, median, or mode, and why a company with a $50,000 "average" salary might pay most people $30,000. I think you'll enjoy it. You've already got the first three tools, so you'll be ready.
